title: Probing the influence of topological and geometric disorder on the spectrum of the differential Laplacian operator on networks
comment: 21 pages and 8 figures in the main text. 13 pages and 20 figures in the supplementary materials
summary: Metric networks are network-shaped, one-dimensional structures on which one can solve differential equations to simulate a wide range of physical systems including conjugated molecules, photonic crystals, quantum mechanics in waveguide networks, and acoustic metamaterials. More concretely, a metric network is a network whose edges are each assigned a notion of length and a coordinate describing position. One can then define function spaces and differential operators on these objects to model the aforementioned systems. Recent software advancements have made it feasible to analyze partial differential equations on large, compact metric networks with a vast array of structures. Here, we generate compact metric network structures using the spatial tessellations of two-dimensional hyperuniform point patterns, which have suppressed large-scale density fluctuations relative to typical disordered point patterns. This choice of structure is inspired by the exotic physical properties of network materials with these structures in other contexts. Then, we characterize the eigenvalue spectrum structure of the differential Laplace operator on these networks. In particular, we find that gaps can form in the eigenvalue spectra of these networks whose widths increase when the distribution of edge lengths is narrow and as the number of triangular faces increases. Importantly, many of the structures we consider are realizable in Euclidean space, meaning they are well-suited for practical applications in, e.g., metamaterial design. This work can thus be used to inform the design of metric network-based systems with spectral gaps with tunable widths and locations.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes eigenvalue spectra of Laplace operators on metric networks generated from hyperuniform point patterns, finding that spectral gaps form with widths tunable by edge length distribution and triangular face count.
AI.motivation: Metric networks enable modeling of various physical systems, but understanding their spectral properties is crucial for applications like metamaterial design. The study aims to characterize eigenvalue spectra of Laplace operators on networks derived from hyperuniform point patterns, which have suppressed density fluctuations and exotic physical properties.
AI.method: Generate compact metric network structures using spatial tessellations of 2D hyperuniform point patterns, then analyze eigenvalue spectrum structure of the differential Laplace operator on these networks. Investigate how spectral gap widths depend on edge length distribution and number of triangular faces.
AI.result: Spectral gaps form in eigenvalue spectra of these networks, with gap widths increasing when edge length distribution is narrow and as the number of triangular faces increases. Many structures are realizable in Euclidean space, making them suitable for practical applications.
AI.conclusion: The work provides insights for designing metric network-based systems with tunable spectral gaps, particularly relevant for metamaterial applications where control over spectral properties is essential.

title: Impact of Stealthy Hyperuniform Magnetic Impurity Configurations on Bulk Magnetism in a Two-dimensional Heisenberg Model
summary: We investigate an antiferromagnetic quantum Heisenberg model on a square lattice with high-spin magnetic impurities to clarify how random and stealthy hyperuniform impurity configurations influence the bulk magnetic properties. Stealthy hyperuniform configurations are generated using generalized cost functions that interpolate between square-lattice-like and triangular-lattice-like arrangements. Using linear spin-wave theory for the mixed-spin model, we demonstrate that triangular-lattice-like arrangements yield a larger average staggered magnetization than both random and square-lattice-like cases. This enhancement originates from sublattice effects: while the square-lattice-like configuration enforces nearest-neighbor impurities to occupy opposite sublattices due to its bipartite structure, the triangular-lattice-like arrangement allows same-sublattice nearest-neighbor pairs, thereby strengthening cooperative magnetic enhancement.

AI.tldr: Triangular-lattice-like hyperuniform impurity arrangements enhance staggered magnetization in antiferromagnetic Heisenberg models compared to random or square-lattice-like configurations due to sublattice effects.
AI.motivation: To understand how different spatial configurations of high-spin magnetic impurities (random vs. stealthy hyperuniform) affect bulk magnetic properties in antiferromagnetic quantum Heisenberg models on square lattices.
AI.method: Linear spin-wave theory applied to mixed-spin models with impurity configurations generated using generalized cost functions that interpolate between square-lattice-like and triangular-lattice-like arrangements.
AI.result: Triangular-lattice-like arrangements yield larger average staggered magnetization than both random and square-lattice-like cases. The enhancement stems from sublattice effects: triangular arrangements allow same-sublattice nearest-neighbor impurity pairs, strengthening cooperative magnetic enhancement.
AI.conclusion: Spatial arrangement of impurities significantly influences magnetic properties, with triangular-lattice-like hyperuniform configurations providing optimal enhancement of staggered magnetization due to favorable sublattice correlations.

title: Exact mapping of a spin glass with correlated disorder to the pure Ising model
summary: We introduce an Ising spin-glass model with correlated disorder which continuously interpolates between the pure ferromagnetic Ising model and the Edwards-Anderson model with symmetric disorder. For this model, we prove that physical quantities on the Nishimori line (NL) can be expressed exactly in terms of those of the pure Ising model at an effective temperature on any lattice in any dimension. For example, the energy on the NL is equal to the energy of the pure Ising model at the effective temperature up to a constant and a trivial factor. More remarkably, the specific heat on the NL equals the energy, not the specific heat, of the pure Ising model at the effective temperature, again up to a constant and a trivial factor. Gauge-noninvariant quantities such as the magnetization and correlation functions are exactly equal to the corresponding quantities of the pure Ising model at the effective temperature. These exact relations imply that the leading critical behavior at that multicritical point for the disorder-correlated model is pure-Ising-like, in contrast to the conventional multicritical universality class of the standard Edwards-Anderson model. Our results motivate further investigations of the relatively unexplored topic of correlations in disorder in spin glasses and related problems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a spin-glass model with correlated disorder that interpolates between pure ferromagnetic Ising and Edwards-Anderson models, proving exact relations between physical quantities on the Nishimori line and those of the pure Ising model at an effective temperature.
AI.motivation: To investigate spin-glass models with correlated disorder, which is relatively unexplored compared to uncorrelated disorder, and to understand how correlations in disorder affect critical behavior and universality classes.
AI.method: Introduces an Ising spin-glass model with correlated disorder that continuously interpolates between pure ferromagnetic Ising and Edwards-Anderson models. Uses gauge theory and the Nishimori line approach to derive exact relations between physical quantities of the correlated disorder model and the pure Ising model at an effective temperature.
AI.result: Proves exact relations: energy on Nishimori line equals pure Ising energy at effective temperature; specific heat equals pure Ising energy (not specific heat) at effective temperature; magnetization and correlation functions equal corresponding pure Ising quantities. Shows leading critical behavior at multicritical point is pure-Ising-like, contrasting with standard Edwards-Anderson universality.
AI.conclusion: The exact relations demonstrate that correlations in disorder can fundamentally change critical behavior, making it pure-Ising-like rather than following conventional spin-glass universality. This motivates further study of correlated disorder in spin glasses and related systems.

title: Dynamics of neural scaling laws in random feature regression with powerlaw-distributed kernel eigenvalues
summary: Training large neural networks exposes neural scaling laws for the generalization error, which points to a universal behavior across network architectures of learning in high dimensions. It was also shown that this effect persists in the limit of highly overparametrized networks as well as the Neural network Gaussian process limit. We here develop a principled understanding of the typical behavior of generalization in Neural Network Gaussian process regression dynamics. We derive a dynamical mean-field theory that captures the typical case learning dynamics: This allows us to unify multiple existing regimes of learning studied in the current literature, namely Bayesian inference on Gaussian processes, gradient flow with or without weight-decay, and stochastic Langevin training dynamics. Employing tools from statistical physics, the unified framework we derive in either of these cases yields an effective description of the high-dimensional microscopic behavior of networks dynamics in terms of lower dimensional order parameters. We show that collective training dynamics may be separated into the dynamics of N independent eigenmodes, those evolution equations are only coupled through collective response functions and a common statistics of an effective, independent noise. Our approach allows us to quantitatively explain the dynamics of the generalization error by linking spectral and dynamical properties of learning on data with power law spectra, including phenomena such as neural scaling laws and the effect of early stopping.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a dynamical mean-field theory to unify different neural network training regimes and explain generalization dynamics, particularly neural scaling laws, through effective low-dimensional descriptions of high-dimensional learning.
AI.motivation: To develop a principled understanding of the typical behavior of generalization in Neural Network Gaussian process regression dynamics, unifying multiple existing training regimes and explaining phenomena like neural scaling laws.
AI.method: Derives a dynamical mean-field theory that captures typical case learning dynamics, employing tools from statistical physics to obtain effective low-dimensional descriptions of high-dimensional network dynamics in terms of order parameters.
AI.result: Shows that collective training dynamics can be separated into independent eigenmodes whose evolution equations are coupled only through collective response functions and common noise statistics, enabling quantitative explanation of generalization error dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The unified framework explains neural scaling laws and early stopping effects by linking spectral and dynamical properties of learning on data with power law spectra, providing a comprehensive theoretical understanding of generalization in high-dimensional neural networks.

title: Stochastic Neural Networks for Quantum Devices
summary: This work presents a formulation to express and optimize stochastic neural networks as quantum circuits in gate-based quantum computing. Motivated by a classical perceptron, stochastic neurons are introduced and combined into a quantum neural network. The Kiefer-Wolfowitz algorithm in combination with simulated annealing is used for training the network weights. Several topologies and models are presented, including shallow fully connected networks, Hopfield Networks, Restricted Boltzmann Machines, Autoencoders and convolutional neural networks. We also demonstrate the combination of our optimized neural networks as an oracle for the Grover algorithm to realize a quantum generative AI model.

AI.tldr: A framework for expressing and optimizing stochastic neural networks as quantum circuits using gate-based quantum computing, with various network architectures and integration with Grover's algorithm for quantum generative AI.
AI.motivation: To bridge classical neural network concepts with quantum computing by formulating stochastic neural networks as quantum circuits, enabling quantum implementations of various neural network architectures and creating quantum generative AI models.
AI.method: Introduces stochastic neurons inspired by classical perceptrons, formulates them as quantum circuits, uses Kiefer-Wolfowitz algorithm with simulated annealing for training weights, implements various network topologies (fully connected, Hopfield, RBM, Autoencoders, CNNs), and combines optimized networks with Grover's algorithm as oracles.
AI.result: Developed a comprehensive framework for quantum implementation of stochastic neural networks across multiple architectures, demonstrated integration with Grover's algorithm to create quantum generative AI models.
AI.conclusion: Successfully established a formulation for quantum neural networks that bridges classical and quantum computing paradigms, enabling quantum implementations of various neural network architectures and opening pathways for quantum generative AI through combination with quantum algorithms like Grover's.

title: Schwinger-Keldysh field theory for operator Rényi entropy and entanglement growth in non-interacting systems with sub-ballistic transports
summary: The notion of operator growth in quantum systems furnishes a bridge between transport and the generation of entanglement between different parts of the system under quantum dynamics. We define a measure of operator growth in terms of subsystem operator Rényi entropy, which provides a state-independent measure of operator growth, unlike entanglement entropies, and the usual measures of operator growth like out-of-time-order correlators. We show that the subsystem operator Rényi entropy encodes both spatial and temporal information, and thus can directly connect to transport for a local operator related to a conserved quantity. We construct a unified Schwinger-Keldysh (SK) field theory formalism for the time evolution of operator Rényi entropy and entanglement entropies of initial pure states. We use the SK field theory to obtain the operator Rényi and state entanglement entropies in terms of infinite-temperature and vacuum Keldysh Green's functions, respectively, for non-interacting systems. We apply the method to explore the connection between operator and entanglement growth, and transport in non-interacting systems with quasiperiodic and random disorder, like the one- and two-dimensional Aubry-André models and the two-dimensional Anderson model. In particular, we show that the growth of subsystem operator Rényi entropy and state von Neumann and Rényi entanglement entropies can capture both ballistic and sub-ballistic transport behaviors, like diffusive and anomalous diffusive transport, as well as localization in these systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces subsystem operator Rényi entropy as a state-independent measure of operator growth, connects it to transport and entanglement, develops a unified Schwinger-Keldysh field theory for operator and entanglement entropies, and applies it to non-interacting disordered systems to capture various transport behaviors.
AI.motivation: To bridge operator growth with transport and entanglement generation in quantum systems, and to develop a unified framework that provides state-independent measures of operator growth beyond traditional approaches like out-of-time-order correlators.
AI.method: Define subsystem operator Rényi entropy as a state-independent measure of operator growth; construct unified Schwinger-Keldysh field theory formalism for time evolution of operator Rényi entropy and entanglement entropies; apply to non-interacting systems using infinite-temperature and vacuum Keldysh Green's functions; analyze one- and two-dimensional Aubry-André models and two-dimensional Anderson model.
AI.result: Subsystem operator Rényi entropy encodes both spatial and temporal information and connects directly to transport for conserved quantities; the SK field theory yields operator and state entropies in terms of Green's functions; the growth of these entropies captures ballistic, sub-ballistic (diffusive, anomalous diffusive) transport behaviors and localization in disordered systems.
AI.conclusion: Subsystem operator Rényi entropy provides a powerful state-independent measure of operator growth that bridges transport, entanglement generation, and operator spreading, with applications to understanding transport behaviors in disordered quantum systems through a unified field-theoretic framework.

title: Robustness-Runtime Tradeoff for Quantum State Transfer
summary: Quantum state transfer is the primitive of transporting an unknown state on one site of a lattice to another. Using power-law interactions, recent state transfer protocols achieve speedup by utilizing the intermediate ancilla sites. However, these protocols require the ancillas to be in a perfectly initialized state, which, due to noise or imperfect control, may not be the case. In this work we introduce the $\textit{robustness}$ of a state transfer protocol, which quantifies the protocol's tolerance to error in the initial ancilla state. In the Heisenberg picture, state transfer grows operators supported on the final site such that they no longer commute with all operators on the starting site. We prove that this robustness tightly bounds the Schatten $p$-norms of these commutators between initial and final-site operators. This generalizes the known cases of $p=\infty$ and $p=2$, which govern completely state-dependent and state-independent state transfer respectively, demonstrating that intermediate values of $p$ govern partially state-dependent state transfer. In conjunction with existing power-law light cones, our result gives new minimum runtimes for partially state-dependent protocols which, in certain regimes, are parametrically better than existing bounds. We introduce new robust state transfer protocols, charting the landscape between complete state-dependence and state-independence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a robustness measure for quantum state transfer protocols that quantifies tolerance to errors in ancilla initialization, connecting it to operator commutator norms and enabling partially state-dependent protocols with improved runtimes.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum state transfer protocols using power-law interactions require perfectly initialized ancilla states, which is unrealistic due to noise and imperfect control. There's a need to quantify and improve protocol tolerance to ancilla initialization errors.
AI.method: Introduces robustness as a measure of protocol tolerance to ancilla initialization errors. Uses Heisenberg picture analysis to prove that robustness tightly bounds Schatten p-norms of commutators between initial and final-site operators. Develops new robust state transfer protocols that span the spectrum between completely state-dependent and state-independent approaches.
AI.result: Establishes that intermediate p-norms (between p=∞ and p=2) govern partially state-dependent state transfer. Derives new minimum runtimes for partially state-dependent protocols using power-law light cones, showing parametric improvements over existing bounds in certain regimes.
AI.conclusion: The robustness framework provides a unified understanding of state transfer protocols across the state-dependence spectrum, enabling the design of more practical protocols that balance speed with tolerance to ancilla initialization errors.

title: Numerical Experiments with Parameter Setting of Trotterized Quantum Phase Estimation for Quantum Hamiltonian Ground State Computation
summary: We numerically investigate quantum circuit elementary-gate level instantiations of the standard Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) algorithm for the task of computing the ground-state energy of a quantum magnet; the disordered fully-connected quantum Heisenberg spin glass model. We consider (classical simulations of) QPE circuit computations on relatively small quantum Hamiltonians ($3$ qubits) with up to $10$ phase bits of precision, using up to Trotter order $10$. We systematically study the inputs of QPE, specifically time evolution, Trotter order, Trotter steps, and initial state, and illustrate how these inputs practically determine how QPE operates. From this we outline a coherent set of quantum algorithm input and tuning guidelines. One of the notable properties we characterize is that QPE sampling of the optimal digitized phase converges to a fixed rate. This results in strong diminishing returns of optimal phase sampling rates which can occur when the Trotter error is surprisingly high.

AI.tldr: Numerical investigation of quantum circuit implementations of Quantum Phase Estimation for computing ground-state energy of disordered quantum Heisenberg spin glass, focusing on input parameter effects and optimization guidelines.
AI.motivation: To understand how various input parameters (time evolution, Trotter order, Trotter steps, initial state) practically determine the operation of QPE algorithms for ground-state energy computation in quantum magnetic systems.
AI.method: Classical simulations of QPE circuits on 3-qubit Hamiltonians with up to 10 phase bits precision, using Trotter orders up to 10, systematically studying QPE inputs and their effects on algorithm performance.
AI.result: Characterization of QPE sampling convergence to fixed rate for optimal digitized phase, revealing strong diminishing returns in optimal phase sampling rates that can occur even with surprisingly high Trotter error.
AI.conclusion: Development of coherent quantum algorithm input and tuning guidelines based on systematic analysis of how QPE inputs practically determine algorithm operation, with insights into optimization trade-offs.

title: Quantum simulation of massive Thirring and Gross--Neveu models for arbitrary number of flavors
summary: The study of fermionic quantum field theories is an important problem for realizing the standard model of particle physics on a quantum computer. As a step towards this goal, we consider the massive Thirring and Gross--Neveu models with arbitrary number of fermion flavors, $N_f$, discretized on a spatial one-dimensional lattice of size $L$ in the Hamiltonian formulation. We compute the gate complexity using the higher-order product formula and using block-encoding/qubitization and quantum singular value transformations in the limit of large $N_f$ and $L$. We also prepare the ground states of both models with excellent fidelity for system sizes up to 20 qubits with $N_f = 1,2,3,4$ using the adaptive-variational quantum imaginary time algorithm. In addition, we also classify the dynamical Lie algebras of these relativistic fermionic models and show that they belong to the same isomorphism class. Our work is a concrete step towards the quantum simulation of real-time dynamics of large $N_f$ fermionic quantum field theories models relevant for chiral symmetry breaking, understanding dimensional transmutation, and exploring the conformal window of field theories on near-term and early fault-tolerant quantum computers.

AI.tldr: Quantum simulation of 1D fermionic QFTs (Thirring/Gross-Neveu) using Hamiltonian formulation, analyzing gate complexity, preparing ground states with adaptive-VQE, and classifying dynamical Lie algebras for near-term quantum computers.
AI.motivation: To advance quantum simulation of fermionic quantum field theories relevant to particle physics, particularly for studying chiral symmetry breaking, dimensional transmutation, and conformal window phenomena on quantum computers.
AI.method: Discretized 1D lattice Hamiltonian formulation of Thirring and Gross-Neveu models; analyzed gate complexity using higher-order product formulas and block-encoding/qubitization; prepared ground states using adaptive-variational quantum imaginary time algorithm; classified dynamical Lie algebras.
AI.result: Successfully prepared ground states with excellent fidelity for systems up to 20 qubits with N_f=1-4; computed gate complexity scaling in large N_f and L limit; showed dynamical Lie algebras of both models belong to same isomorphism class.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrated concrete progress toward quantum simulation of real-time dynamics in fermionic QFTs, providing tools and analysis for implementation on near-term and early fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Taxonomy of Integrable and Ground-State Solvable Models: Jastrow Wavefunctions on Graphs and Parent Hamiltonians
summary: We introduce a family of many-body systems of distinguishable continuous-variable particles in which interparticle interactions are set by the adjacency matrix of a graph. The ground-state wavefunction of such systems is of a generalized Jastrow form involving the product of pair-correlation functions over the edge set of the graph. These systems describe quantum fluids when the graph is complete, and the pair function has a well-defined permutation symmetry. In general, they provide the continuous-variable generalization of spin systems on graphs, with broken permutation symmetry. The corresponding parent Hamiltonian is shown to include (a) two-body interactions determined by the graph adjacency matrix and (b) three-body interactions over all possible 2-paths on the graph. Employing elements of graph theory, we chart the landscape of models, recovering known instances in the literature and providing numerous new examples of ground-state solvable models for which the system Hamiltonian, ground-state wavefunction, and corresponding energy eigenvalue are specified.

AI.tldr: Continuous-variable quantum systems on graphs with generalized Jastrow ground states and parent Hamiltonians containing two-body and three-body interactions.
AI.motivation: To develop a general framework for many-body continuous-variable systems where interparticle interactions are determined by graph adjacency matrices, extending beyond complete graphs (quantum fluids) to arbitrary graphs with broken permutation symmetry.
AI.method: Introduce family of systems with ground-state wavefunctions of generalized Jastrow form involving products of pair-correlation functions over graph edges. Derive parent Hamiltonians containing: (a) two-body interactions determined by adjacency matrix, and (b) three-body interactions over all possible 2-paths on the graph.
AI.result: Chart landscape of models using graph theory, recovering known instances from literature and providing numerous new examples of ground-state solvable models where Hamiltonian, ground-state wavefunction, and energy eigenvalue are explicitly specified.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides continuous-variable generalization of spin systems on graphs with broken permutation symmetry, establishing connections between graph structure and many-body quantum systems while expanding the class of exactly solvable models.

title: Partial Reversibility and Counterdiabatic Driving in Nearly Integrable Systems
summary: Adiabatic (or reversible) processes are the key concept unifying our understanding of thermodynamics and dynamical systems. Reversibility in the thermodynamic sense is understood as entropy-preserving processes, such as in the idealized Carnot engine, whereas in integrable dynamical systems it is understood as the conservation of the action variables. Between these two idealized limits, however, where the phase space can become mixed, things are much less clear. In this work, we first determine the extent to which reversible processes are even possible in this regime. We then explore how the dissipative losses resulting from rapidly driving these kinds of systems can be fought by approximate counterdiabatic driving. Finally, we argue that much of the phenomenology should be the same for quantum many-body systems with large degeneracy in the presence of integrability breaking perturbations.

AI.tldr: The paper explores reversible processes in mixed phase space systems, bridging thermodynamics and dynamical systems, and examines counterdiabatic driving to mitigate dissipative losses.
AI.motivation: To understand reversible processes in the intermediate regime between idealized thermodynamic reversibility (entropy-preserving) and integrable dynamical systems (action conservation), where phase space becomes mixed and the concept is less clear.
AI.method: First determines the extent of possible reversible processes in mixed phase space regimes, then explores using approximate counterdiabatic driving to combat dissipative losses from rapid driving, and extends analysis to quantum many-body systems with large degeneracy under integrability-breaking perturbations.
AI.result: The paper establishes limitations on reversible processes in mixed phase space systems and demonstrates how counterdiabatic driving can reduce dissipative losses, with similar phenomenology expected for quantum many-body systems with degeneracy under integrability breaking.
AI.conclusion: Reversible processes in mixed phase space are constrained but can be approximated using counterdiabatic techniques, with implications extending to quantum many-body systems, bridging thermodynamic and dynamical system perspectives on reversibility.

title: Fundamental Limits on QBER and Distance in Quantum Key Distribution
comment: REVTeX 7 pages. 1 Figure. Feedback is welcome
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) enables information-theoretic secure communication, yet its ultimate tolerance to noise and achievable transmission distance remain fundamentally constrained. We establish the maximum quantum bit error rate (QBER) compatible with secure QKD and derive corresponding upper bounds on communication distance. Our results follow from a fundamental capacity threshold for qubit Pauli channels and apply to protocols based on two or more mutually unbiased bases, using either single-photon or weak coherent sources. By connecting information-theoretic limits to realistic physical noise models, we obtain universal bounds on achievable distances in fiber and free-space links, including diffraction-limited constraints relevant to deep-space quantum communications. These findings clarify the ultimate noise robustness of QKD and delineate the fundamental boundaries of secure quantum communication.

AI.tldr: Fundamental limits on QKD noise tolerance and transmission distance derived from qubit Pauli channel capacity thresholds, establishing maximum QBER and universal bounds for fiber/free-space links.
AI.motivation: Quantum key distribution enables information-theoretic security but has fundamental limitations in noise tolerance and transmission distance that need to be precisely characterized.
AI.method: Derived maximum quantum bit error rate (QBER) compatible with secure QKD from fundamental capacity thresholds for qubit Pauli channels, applicable to protocols using two or more mutually unbiased bases with single-photon or weak coherent sources.
AI.result: Established ultimate noise robustness limits for QKD, derived corresponding upper bounds on communication distance, and obtained universal bounds for fiber and free-space links including diffraction-limited constraints for deep-space communications.
AI.conclusion: The findings clarify the fundamental boundaries of secure quantum communication by connecting information-theoretic limits to realistic physical noise models, delineating the ultimate achievable distances for QKD systems.

title: Symmetry-protected control of Liouvillian topological phases via Hamiltonian band topology
summary: We establish a symmetry-protected correspondence between band topology of coherent Hamiltonians and Liouvillian spectral winding in Lindblad descriptions of open quantum systems. This allows the Hamiltonian topology to act as a knob for controlling Liouvillian topology and corresponding non-equilibrium dynamics, rather than being passively manipulated by system-environment exchanges. In particular, by exactly solving the Liouvillian spectrum in a class of one-dimensional dissipative lattices, we find that the Hamiltonian band topology constrains the Liouvillian spectral winding and determines the Liouvillian skin effect, provided the Hamiltonian and quantum jump operators respect the same chiral symmetry. We further demonstrate that lattice parity controls the associated bulk-boundary correspondence and the coherence properties of the steady state. Our results unveil a symmetry-enforced topological control of spectral and spatial organization in open quantum systems, providing a unified perspective on topology in Hamiltonian and dissipative dynamics.

AI.tldr: Hamiltonian band topology controls Liouvillian spectral winding and skin effects in open quantum systems via symmetry protection.
AI.motivation: To establish an active relationship where Hamiltonian topology controls dissipative dynamics rather than being passively affected by system-environment interactions.
AI.method: Exact solution of Liouvillian spectrum in 1D dissipative lattices, analyzing symmetry constraints between Hamiltonian and quantum jump operators.
AI.result: Hamiltonian band topology constrains Liouvillian spectral winding and determines Liouvillian skin effect when Hamiltonian and jump operators share chiral symmetry; lattice parity controls bulk-boundary correspondence and steady-state coherence.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry-enforced topological control provides unified perspective on topology in both Hamiltonian and dissipative dynamics, enabling active manipulation of open quantum system properties.

title: The unbearable hardness of deciding about magic
summary: Identifying the boundary between classical and quantum computation is a central challenge in quantum information. In multi-qubit systems, entanglement and magic are the key resources underlying genuinely quantum behaviour. While entanglement is well understood, magic -- essential for universal quantum computation -- remains relatively poorly characterised. Here we show that determining membership in the stabilizer polytope, which defines the free states of magic-state resource theory, requires super-exponential time $\exp( n^2)$ in the number of qubits $n$, even approximately. We reduce the problem to solving a $3$-SAT instance on $n^2$ variables and, by invoking the exponential time hypothesis, the result follows. As a consequence, both quantifying and certifying magic are fundamentally intractable: any magic monotone for general states must be super-exponentially hard to compute, and deciding whether an operator is a valid magic witness is equally difficult. As a corollary, we establish the robustness of magic as computationally optimal among monotones. This barrier extends even to classically simulable regimes: deciding whether a state lies in the convex hull of states generated by a logarithmic number of non-Clifford gates is also super-exponentially hard. Together, these results reveal intrinsic computational limits on assessing classical simulability, distilling pathological magic states, and ultimately probing and exploiting magic as a quantum resource.

AI.tldr: Determining membership in the stabilizer polytope (free states of magic-state resource theory) requires super-exponential time exp(n²) in qubit number n, establishing fundamental computational limits on quantifying and certifying magic.
AI.motivation: To understand the boundary between classical and quantum computation by characterizing magic (non-stabilizer resources), which is essential for universal quantum computation but remains poorly characterized compared to entanglement.
AI.method: Reduced the problem of determining membership in the stabilizer polytope to solving a 3-SAT instance on n² variables, then invoked the exponential time hypothesis to establish super-exponential time complexity exp(n²).
AI.result: Both quantifying and certifying magic are fundamentally intractable: any magic monotone for general states must be super-exponentially hard to compute, and deciding whether an operator is a valid magic witness is equally difficult. The robustness of magic is established as computationally optimal among monotones.
AI.conclusion: Reveals intrinsic computational limits on assessing classical simulability, distilling pathological magic states, and probing/exploiting magic as a quantum resource, even extending to classically simulable regimes with logarithmic non-Clifford gates.

title: Basis-independent stabilizerness and maximally noisy magic states
summary: Absolutely stabilizer states are those that remain convex mixtures of stabilizer states after conjugation by any unitary. Here we give a characterization of such states for multiple qudits of all prime dimensions by introducing a polytope of their allowed spectra. We illustrate this through the examples of one qubit, two qubits, and one qutrit. In particular, the set of absolutely stabilizer states for a single qubit is a ball inscribed in the stabilizer octahedron, but for higher dimensions the geometry is more complicated. For odd-prime-dimensional qudits, we also give a complete characterization of absolutely Wigner-positive states, i.e., states whose Wigner function remains nonnegative after conjugation by any unitary. In so doing, we show there are absolutely Wigner-positive states that are not absolutely stabilizer, which can be seen as a unitarily-invariant version of bound magic. We then study the radii of the largest balls contained in the sets of absolutely stabilizer states and absolutely Wigner-positive states. These radii respectively tell us the lowest possible purity of nonstabilizer and Wigner-negative states. Conversely, we also find the radius of the smallest ball containing the set of absolutely Wigner-positive states, giving a tight purity-based necessary condition thereof.

AI.tldr: Characterization of absolutely stabilizer states (states remaining convex mixtures of stabilizer states under any unitary) via spectral polytopes for prime-dimensional qudits, with geometric analysis and purity bounds.
AI.motivation: To understand which quantum states maintain their stabilizer or Wigner-positive character under arbitrary unitary transformations, providing a unitarily-invariant notion of "bound magic" and establishing fundamental purity limits for non-stabilizer and Wigner-negative states.
AI.method: Introduce polytope of allowed spectra for absolutely stabilizer states; characterize absolutely Wigner-positive states for odd-prime dimensions; analyze geometric properties (inscribed/containing balls) to derive purity bounds; illustrate with examples (qubit, two qubits, qutrit).
AI.result: For single qubit: absolutely stabilizer states form ball inscribed in stabilizer octahedron; for higher dimensions geometry more complex. Existence of absolutely Wigner-positive states not absolutely stabilizer (unitarily-invariant bound magic). Derived radii of largest balls in absolutely stabilizer/Wigner-positive sets (giving lowest purity of non-stabilizer/Wigner-negative states) and radius of smallest ball containing absolutely Wigner-positive states (tight purity-based necessary condition).
AI.conclusion: Complete characterization of absolutely stabilizer and Wigner-positive states for prime-dimensional qudits, revealing geometric structure and establishing fundamental purity-based limitations, with implications for understanding magic states and resource theories in quantum computation.

title: A field-biased HPZ master equation and its Markovian limit
summary: We present a first-principles derivation of a non-equilibrium quantum master equation for a continuously driven open quantum system interacting with a structured electromagnetic environment. Starting from a driven Caldeira-Leggett model in which an external classical field couples simultaneously to the system and reservoir degrees of freedom, we proceed without assuming that the standard equilibrium fluctuation-dissipation theorem holds. The bath statistics acquire explicit dependence on the two-time autocorrelation function of the applied field, leading to drive-biased noise correlations and intrinsically non-Markovian dynamics. By eliminating the reservoir exactly at the operator level, we obtain a driven quantum generalized Langevin equation whose noise and dissipation kernels depend on two independent times. Exploiting the Gaussian nature of the driven bath, we derive a modified Hu-Paz-Zhang master equation in which the diffusion coefficients and coherent forces inherit explicit memory of the external field. We demonstrate that the physically observable oscillation frequency remains encoded in the homogeneous Green's function of the Langevin equation, while the drive-induced corrections manifest exclusively through modified diffusion and drift terms. Our results provide a unified microscopic framework for understanding field-biased fluctuation relations with direct relevance to cavity and circuit quantum electrodynamics experiments operating far from equilibrium.

AI.tldr: First-principles derivation of non-equilibrium quantum master equation for driven open quantum systems with structured electromagnetic environments, revealing drive-biased noise correlations and non-Markovian dynamics.
AI.motivation: To establish a microscopic framework for understanding driven open quantum systems far from equilibrium, particularly relevant to cavity and circuit QED experiments where standard equilibrium assumptions fail due to continuous driving.
AI.method: Start from driven Caldeira-Leggett model with external classical field coupling to both system and reservoir. Eliminate reservoir exactly at operator level to obtain driven quantum generalized Langevin equation. Exploit Gaussian nature of driven bath to derive modified Hu-Paz-Zhang master equation with field-dependent diffusion coefficients and coherent forces.
AI.result: Derived master equation shows bath statistics acquire explicit dependence on two-time autocorrelation function of applied field, leading to drive-biased noise correlations and intrinsically non-Markovian dynamics. Observable oscillation frequency remains encoded in homogeneous Green's function, while drive-induced corrections manifest through modified diffusion and drift terms.
AI.conclusion: Provides unified microscopic framework for understanding field-biased fluctuation relations in driven open quantum systems, with direct relevance to far-from-equilibrium cavity and circuit QED experiments.

title: Macroscopic Quantum Electrodynamics with Gain: Modified Fluctuations and Their Consequences
summary: Macroscopic quantum electrodynamics (MQED) provides a unified framework to describe quantum electromagnetic fields in the presence of arbitrary macroscopic environments. Central to this theory is the field correlation, which governs both radiative (e.g., Lamb shifts and the Purcell effect) and mechanical phenomena, such as van der Waals and Casimir forces. In this tutorial, we provide an overview of MQED and its extension to active media, highlighting fluctuation-induced forces as manifestations of gain-modified field correlations.

AI.tldr: Tutorial overview of macroscopic quantum electrodynamics (MQED) framework for quantum electromagnetic fields in macroscopic environments, focusing on field correlations governing radiative and mechanical phenomena, with extension to active media and gain-modified fluctuation-induced forces.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive tutorial on MQED, which offers a unified framework for describing quantum electromagnetic fields in arbitrary macroscopic environments, and to extend this framework to active media where gain modifies field correlations and fluctuation-induced forces.
AI.method: Tutorial approach presenting the MQED theoretical framework, focusing on field correlations as central elements that govern both radiative phenomena (Lamb shifts, Purcell effect) and mechanical phenomena (van der Waals, Casimir forces), with extension to active media.
AI.result: The tutorial provides an overview of MQED and demonstrates how fluctuation-induced forces emerge as manifestations of gain-modified field correlations in active media, highlighting the unified description of quantum electromagnetic phenomena in macroscopic environments.
AI.conclusion: MQED provides a powerful unified framework for quantum electrodynamics in macroscopic environments, with field correlations serving as the fundamental quantity governing both radiative and mechanical phenomena, and this framework can be extended to active media where gain modifies these correlations and associated forces.

title: Revisiting the Role of State Texture in Gate Identification and Fixed-Point Resource Theories
summary: A protocol for identifying controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates versus single-qubit-only gates in universal quantum circuits using randomized input states was recently shown to be intimately connected to the quantum resource of state texture. Here we revisit this gate identification protocol and demonstrate that a more general fidelity-based formulation succeeds for nearly all laboratory bases. We then examine a broader family of quantum resource theories, where a distinct resource theory can be defined for each choice of reference pure state, establishing core resource-theoretic requirements without the computational shortcut offered by the "grand sum" employed in the original formulation of state texture. By extending from single "resourceless" states to convex sets via a convex-roof construction, we recover single-qubit measures of known resource theories such as imaginarity and coherence. Finally, we introduce a family of "fixed-point resource theories" that includes fixed-point instances of the theories of state texture, genuine coherence, purity, and athermality. For these fixed-point resource theories we show that, under free operations, the fidelity-based lower bound is weakly monotonic, while specific violations of strong monotonicity are found for the convex-roof logarithmic measure.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits a CNOT gate identification protocol, generalizes it using fidelity-based formulation, extends state texture resource theory to broader family of resource theories with convex-roof construction, and introduces fixed-point resource theories with monotonicity analysis.
AI.motivation: To revisit and improve upon a previously established protocol for identifying CNOT gates versus single-qubit gates in quantum circuits, and to extend the underlying resource theory framework (state texture) to a broader family of quantum resource theories.
AI.method: 1) Reformulate the gate identification protocol using fidelity-based approach that works for nearly all laboratory bases; 2) Define broader family of resource theories where each reference pure state defines a distinct theory; 3) Extend from single resourceless states to convex sets via convex-roof construction; 4) Introduce fixed-point resource theories as specific instances; 5) Analyze monotonicity properties of fidelity-based lower bounds and convex-roof logarithmic measures.
AI.result: 1) Fidelity-based formulation succeeds for nearly all laboratory bases; 2) Convex-roof construction recovers known single-qubit measures like imaginarity and coherence; 3) Fixed-point resource theories include instances of state texture, genuine coherence, purity, and athermality; 4) Fidelity-based lower bound is weakly monotonic under free operations; 5) Specific violations of strong monotonicity are found for convex-roof logarithmic measure.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully generalizes the CNOT gate identification protocol and establishes a comprehensive framework for broader quantum resource theories, providing insights into monotonicity properties and connecting various known resource theories through a unified convex-roof construction approach.

title: Quantified convergence of general homodyne measurements with applications to continuous variable quantum computing
summary: In arXiv:2503.00188 we introduced broadband pulsed (BBP) homodyne measurements as a generalization of standard pulsed homodyne quadrature measurements. BBP can take advantage of detectors such as calorimeters that have the potential for high efficiency over a broad spectral range. BBP homodyne retains the advantages of standard pulsed homodyne, enabling measurement of arbitrary quadratures in the limit of large amplitude local oscillators (LO). Here we quantify the convergence of standard and BBP homodyne quadrature measurements to those of the quadrature of interest. We obtain lower bounds on the fidelity of the post-measurement classical-quantum state of outcomes and unmeasured modes, and the fidelity of the states obtained after applying operations conditional on measurement outcomes. The bounds depend on the LO amplitude and the moments of number operators. We demonstrate the practical relevance of these bounds by evaluating them for standard pulsed homodyne used for estimating values of the characteristic function of the Wigner distribution, expectations of moments, for quantum teleportation and for continuous variable error correction with GKP codes.

AI.tldr: Broadband pulsed (BBP) homodyne measurements generalize standard pulsed homodyne, enabling use of broadband detectors like calorimeters while maintaining arbitrary quadrature measurement capability with large LO amplitudes.
AI.motivation: To quantify convergence of both standard and BBP homodyne measurements to ideal quadrature measurements, establishing performance bounds for practical quantum information applications.
AI.method: Derived lower bounds on fidelity of post-measurement classical-quantum states and conditional operations, expressed in terms of LO amplitude and number operator moments.
AI.result: Obtained practical fidelity bounds applicable to key quantum information tasks: estimating Wigner characteristic functions, expectation values, quantum teleportation, and GKP error correction.
AI.conclusion: BBP homodyne measurements provide a viable alternative to standard pulsed homodyne with broadband detector compatibility, with quantifiable performance bounds for practical quantum applications.

title: Gravitational decoherence and recoherence of a composite particle: the interplay between gravitons and a classical Newtonian potential
summary: The fact that gravitational environments cannot be shielded (since gravity is universal) makes them of great theoretical interest to decoherence mechanisms and to the quantum-to-classical transition. While past results seemed to indicate that graviton-induced decoherence of spatial superpositions happens only for macroscopic systems, recently it was shown that this mechanism can be enhanced through the system's own dynamical internal structure. In this work, we extend this analysis by including the interaction with a classical Newtonian potential. We show that, although the graviton bath alone dominates the mechanism for short times compared to a timescale established by the size of the quantum spatial superposition, the interplay between the gravitons and the internal degrees of freedom of the system renders decoherence inevitable in the long-time limit, even for microscopic masses. We also show that this mechanism is slightly slowed down by the interplay with the classical Newtonian potential, which, for systems without dynamical internal degrees of freedom, can even lead to recoherence, at least in principle.

AI.tldr: Gravitational decoherence of spatial superpositions is enhanced by a system's internal dynamics, making decoherence inevitable even for microscopic masses, though classical Newtonian potential can slow it down.
AI.motivation: To understand how gravitational environments (which cannot be shielded) contribute to decoherence and the quantum-to-classical transition, particularly extending previous work that showed graviton-induced decoherence can be enhanced through a system's internal structure.
AI.method: Extends previous analysis by including interaction with a classical Newtonian potential, examining the interplay between gravitons, internal degrees of freedom, and classical gravity to study decoherence dynamics.
AI.result: Graviton bath dominates decoherence for short times compared to superposition size, but interplay with internal degrees makes decoherence inevitable in long-time limit even for microscopic masses. Classical Newtonian potential slightly slows this mechanism and can lead to recoherence for systems without internal dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Internal dynamics of quantum systems play crucial role in gravitational decoherence, ensuring eventual decoherence even for microscopic systems, though classical gravitational interactions can modify the timescale and potentially cause recoherence in simpler systems.

title: The Road to Useful Quantum Computers
comment: This article was written by invitation for the National Academy of Engineering (NAE)'s magazine, The Bridge, based on a talk given by the first author at The Grainger Foundation Frontiers of Engineering 2025 Symposium. It was written for a general audience of engineers. It is close to the published article, which can be found at https://www.nae.edu/344306/the-road-to-useful-quantum-computers
summary: Building a useful quantum computer is a grand science and engineering challenge, currently pursued intensely by teams around the world. In the 1980s, Richard Feynman and Yuri Manin observed independently that computers based on quantum mechanics might enable better simulations of quantum phenomena. Their vision remained an intellectual curiosity until Peter Shor published his famous quantum algorithm for integer factoring, and shortly thereafter a proof that errors in quantum computations can be corrected. Since then, quantum computing R&D has progressed rapidly, from small-scale experiments in university physics laboratories to well-funded industrial efforts and prototypes. Hype notwithstanding, quantum computers have yet to solve scientifically or practically important problems -- a target often called quantum utility. In this article, we describe the capabilities of contemporary quantum computers, compare them to the requirements of quantum utility, and illustrate how to track progress from today to utility. We highlight key science and engineering challenges on the road to quantum utility, touching on relevant aspects of our own research.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a comprehensive overview of quantum computing's evolution from theoretical concept to current industrial development, analyzes the gap between present capabilities and quantum utility, and outlines a framework for tracking progress toward practical quantum applications.
AI.motivation: To assess the current state of quantum computing, identify the gap between existing capabilities and quantum utility (solving scientifically or practically important problems), and provide a framework for tracking progress toward achieving practical quantum applications.
AI.method: The authors describe contemporary quantum computer capabilities, compare them to quantum utility requirements, illustrate methods for tracking progress from current state to utility, and highlight key science and engineering challenges based on their own research.
AI.result: The paper establishes that while quantum computing has progressed significantly from theoretical origins to industrial prototypes, current systems have not yet achieved quantum utility - the ability to solve scientifically or practically important problems that classical computers cannot.
AI.conclusion: Quantum computing remains an active research frontier with substantial challenges ahead; achieving quantum utility requires overcoming key scientific and engineering obstacles, and systematic progress tracking is essential for advancing from current prototypes to practically useful quantum computers.

title: Optimizing Doppler laser cooling protocols for quantum sensing with 3D ion crystals in a Penning trap
summary: Large, 3D trapped ion crystals offer improved sensitivity in quantum sensing protocols, and are expected to be implemented as platforms in near-future experiments. However, numerical techniques used to study the laser cooling of such crystals are inefficient as the number of ions, $N$, in the crystal increases. Here we develop a powerful numerical framework to simulate laser cooling of up to $10^5$ ions stored in a Penning trap. We apply this framework to characterize and optimize the cooling of ellipsoidal 3D crystals. We document new pathways to enhanced cooling based on the addition of an axial component to the potential energy-dominated $\boldsymbol{E}\times\boldsymbol{B}$ modes. Furthermore, we observe greatly enhanced cooling of the perpendicular kinetic energy to below 1 mK in prolate ion crystals, enabling a simplified cooling beam setup for such crystals. We propose specific values of trap and laser beam parameters which lead to optimal cooling in a variety of examples. This work illustrates the feasibility of preparing large 3D crystals for high-sensitivity quantum science protocols, motivating their use in future experiments.

AI.tldr: A numerical framework for simulating laser cooling of up to 10^5 ions in Penning traps enables optimization of 3D ellipsoidal crystal cooling, revealing enhanced cooling pathways and proposing optimal parameters for quantum sensing applications.
AI.motivation: Large 3D trapped ion crystals offer improved sensitivity for quantum sensing, but existing numerical techniques for studying their laser cooling become inefficient as crystal size increases, creating a need for more powerful simulation methods.
AI.method: Developed a powerful numerical framework to simulate laser cooling of up to 10^5 ions stored in Penning traps, applied to characterize and optimize cooling of ellipsoidal 3D crystals, focusing on adding axial components to E×B modes.
AI.result: Discovered new pathways to enhanced cooling through axial component addition to E×B modes, achieved greatly enhanced cooling of perpendicular kinetic energy to below 1 mK in prolate crystals, and proposed specific optimal trap and laser beam parameters.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates feasibility of preparing large 3D crystals for high-sensitivity quantum science protocols, enabling simplified cooling beam setups and motivating their use in future quantum sensing experiments.

title: Loss-insensitive quantum noise reduction in a Raman amplifier with coherent feedback
summary: A quantum amplifier usually adds extra noise inevitably through coupling to internal degrees of freedom while amplifying the signal. The introduction of quantum correlations can effectively suppress this extra noise. In this work, we utilize the established quantum correlation between the Stokes field and atomic spin waves in the Raman amplification process to feedback a portion of the Stokes field into the amplifier. This leads to a reduction in quantum noise that is independent of the feedback loss at high gain. A maximum of 6 dB noise reduction is observed. The single-path feedback amplifier is found to be sensitive to the feedback phase, a property that expands its potential for applications in quantum precision measurement, and the general concept can be extended to integrated optics and fiber optic systems.

AI.tldr: Quantum amplifier with Stokes field feedback reduces noise by 6dB using quantum correlations in Raman amplification process.
AI.motivation: Quantum amplifiers inevitably add extra noise through coupling to internal degrees of freedom, and quantum correlations can effectively suppress this noise.
AI.method: Utilize established quantum correlation between Stokes field and atomic spin waves in Raman amplification process to feedback a portion of the Stokes field into the amplifier, creating a single-path feedback amplifier sensitive to feedback phase.
AI.result: Reduction in quantum noise independent of feedback loss at high gain, with maximum 6 dB noise reduction observed.
AI.conclusion: The feedback amplifier's sensitivity to feedback phase expands its potential for quantum precision measurement applications, and the general concept can be extended to integrated optics and fiber optic systems.

title: SYK thermal expectations are classically easy at any temperature
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures; 34 pages of supplemental material
summary: Estimating thermal expectations of local observables is a natural target for quantum advantage. We give a simple classical algorithm that approximates thermal expectations, and we show it has quasi-polynomial cost $n^{O(\log n/ε)}$ for all temperatures above a phase transition in the free energy. For many natural models, this coincides with the entire fast-mixing, quantumly easy phase. Our results apply to the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model at any constant temperature -- including when the thermal state is highly entangled and satisfies polynomial quantum circuit lower bounds, a sign problem, and nontrivial instance-to-instance fluctuations. Our analysis of the SYK model relies on the replica trick to control the complex zeros of the partition function.

AI.tldr: Classical algorithm approximates thermal expectations with quasi-polynomial cost above phase transition, applicable to SYK model at all constant temperatures despite quantum complexity.
AI.motivation: Thermal expectation estimation is a natural target for quantum advantage, but the authors aim to show classical algorithms can achieve this for certain regimes, particularly for models like SYK that exhibit quantum complexity.
AI.method: Develop a simple classical algorithm with quasi-polynomial cost $n^{O(\log n/ε)}$ that works above a phase transition in free energy. For SYK model analysis, use replica trick to control complex zeros of partition function.
AI.result: Algorithm achieves quasi-polynomial cost for all temperatures above phase transition, covering entire fast-mixing, quantumly easy phase for many natural models. Applies to SYK model at any constant temperature, even when thermal state is highly entangled with polynomial quantum circuit lower bounds.
AI.conclusion: Classical algorithms can efficiently approximate thermal expectations in regimes previously thought to require quantum advantage, challenging assumptions about quantum computational supremacy for certain thermal estimation tasks.

title: Vibration induced transparency and absorption with two ion ensembles in a linear trap
summary: We study the spectra of collective low excitations of two atomic ion ensembles which are confined in a liner trap by addressing lases. When the left ensemble is driven by an external optical field, its corresponding response spectrum to the incident optical light shows a vibration-induced transparency phenomenon when the detuning of the laser addressing the ion is tuned to the first red sideband. In the case of the detuning tuned to the first blue sideband, the response spectrum shows a conversion from the absorption peak to the transparency window. Furthermore, we investigate the fluctuation spectra of the collective excitation modes of ion ensemble and show the similar phenomena.

AI.tldr: Study of collective low excitations in two atomic ion ensembles shows vibration-induced transparency phenomena in response spectra when driven by external optical fields at specific sideband detunings.
AI.motivation: To investigate the spectral properties of collective low excitations in trapped ion ensembles when subjected to external optical driving fields, particularly focusing on how vibrational modes affect optical response spectra.
AI.method: Two atomic ion ensembles confined in a linear trap are addressed with lasers. The left ensemble is driven by an external optical field, and response spectra are analyzed when laser detuning is tuned to first red and blue sidebands. Fluctuation spectra of collective excitation modes are also investigated.
AI.result: When detuning is tuned to first red sideband, response spectrum shows vibration-induced transparency phenomenon. When tuned to first blue sideband, spectrum shows conversion from absorption peak to transparency window. Similar phenomena observed in fluctuation spectra of collective excitation modes.
AI.conclusion: Vibrational sideband transitions in trapped ion ensembles can induce transparency phenomena in optical response spectra, with different behaviors observed for red versus blue sideband excitations, suggesting potential applications in quantum optics and quantum information processing.

title: Finite key analysis of experimentally realized practical COW-QKD protocol
comment: Finite key analysis of the COW-QKD protocol is performed to obtain realistic security bounds
summary: An experimental implementation of the Coherent One-Way Quantum Key Distribution (COW-QKD) protocol is reported under realistic conditions, and a clean and easy-to-use framework for performing finite key analysis of the COW-QKD protocol is provided by extending a set of existing results. The framework provided here is used to perform finite key rate analysis of the COW-QKD protocol with respect to the actual parameters used in the experimental realization reported here. The system is kept running for several hours with different experimental parameters and stable secure key rates between 1.2 to 1.6 kbps are observed. In addition, QBER, phase error rate and secure key rate are obtained under finite key analysis, and it is shown that COW-QKD is secure for medium-range transmissions (up-to ~ 156 (171) km of optical fiber with 0.2 dB loss per km if detector efficiency is 0.1 (0.2) and other parameters are same as those used in this experiment).

AI.tldr: Experimental implementation and finite key analysis of COW-QKD protocol showing stable key rates of 1.2-1.6 kbps and security for medium-range transmissions up to ~156-171 km.
AI.motivation: To experimentally implement the COW-QKD protocol under realistic conditions and provide a practical framework for finite key analysis, addressing the gap between theoretical security proofs and practical implementations.
AI.method: Experimental implementation of COW-QKD protocol with extended finite key analysis framework using existing results. System operated for several hours with varying parameters, measuring QBER, phase error rates, and secure key rates.
AI.result: Stable secure key rates between 1.2 to 1.6 kbps achieved. Finite key analysis shows COW-QKD secure for medium-range transmissions up to ~156 km (with 0.1 detector efficiency) or 171 km (with 0.2 detector efficiency) over optical fiber with 0.2 dB/km loss.
AI.conclusion: COW-QKD protocol is experimentally viable under realistic conditions with practical secure key rates and can be secured for medium-range transmissions using finite key analysis, demonstrating its potential for real-world quantum key distribution applications.

title: Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation with Quantum Feedback
summary: Fluctuations are intrinsic to microscopic systems and impose fundamental limits on nonequilibrium precision, as captured by the thermodynamic uncertainty relation (TUR), which links current fluctuations to entropy production. While feedback control is expected to further suppress fluctuations, its role within the TUR framework has remained unclear, particularly in quantum systems where control is inherently information-driven. In this Letter, we consider open quantum systems weakly coupled to a thermal environment, in which quantum jumps are continuously monitored, and Markovian feedback is applied. Using quantum mutual information to quantify the information contribution induced by feedback, we derive a finite-time TUR for arbitrary time-integrated currents in terms of entropy production and mutual information. Our results uncover how feedback control suppresses fluctuations together with thermodynamic cost and establishes a fundamental precision bound imposed by information-based control. As an application, we analyze a quantum clock model and demonstrate that the clock precision can be enhanced by feedback control in the presence of a single thermal reservoir.

AI.tldr: Quantum thermodynamic uncertainty relation incorporating feedback control via mutual information, showing how information-based control suppresses fluctuations and enhances precision in quantum systems.
AI.motivation: Feedback control is expected to suppress fluctuations in microscopic systems, but its role within the thermodynamic uncertainty relation (TUR) framework remains unclear, especially in quantum systems where control is inherently information-driven.
AI.method: Consider open quantum systems weakly coupled to thermal environments with continuous monitoring of quantum jumps and application of Markovian feedback. Use quantum mutual information to quantify information contribution from feedback, deriving a finite-time TUR for arbitrary time-integrated currents in terms of entropy production and mutual information.
AI.result: Derived a TUR incorporating feedback control that reveals how feedback suppresses fluctuations together with thermodynamic cost, establishing fundamental precision bounds for information-based control. Applied to quantum clock model showing feedback can enhance clock precision even with single thermal reservoir.
AI.conclusion: Feedback control in quantum systems can be quantified via mutual information within the TUR framework, providing fundamental bounds on precision achievable through information-based control and demonstrating practical applications like enhanced quantum clock precision.

title: Quantum-Optically Resolving the Number of Colloidal Quantum Dots in a Subwavelength Volume
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures. Main text includes methods
summary: The number resolution of solid-state artificial atoms is of fundamental interest for the study of quantum few-body systems, yet remains experimentally challenging. Quantum optical experiments offer a non-invasive approach which links up macroscopic measurements with the quantity of quantum emitters. In this work, we propose a time-domain quantum optical methodology for the strict numbering of colloidal CdSe/CdS/ZnS quantum dots (QDs) confined in subwavelength-size polystyrene capsules. The non-polarized, homogeneously broadened emission of colloidal QDs in the subwavelength volume satisfies the description of Dicke's superradiance of identical quantum emitters. An analytic relation describes the numerical dependence of the second-order photon correlation on the number and the collective lifetime of emitters, yielding an experimental counting range of colloidal QDs from one to ten. This work provides a robust pathway for the non-invasive numbering of artificial atoms and the investigation of collective light-matter interactions at the nanoscale.

AI.tldr: A quantum optical method for non-invasively counting colloidal quantum dots (1-10) in subwavelength capsules using time-domain photon correlation measurements and Dicke superradiance theory.
AI.motivation: Resolving the exact number of solid-state artificial atoms (quantum dots) is fundamental for studying quantum few-body systems but experimentally challenging. Quantum optics offers a non-invasive approach to link macroscopic measurements with quantum emitter quantities.
AI.method: Time-domain quantum optical methodology for counting colloidal CdSe/CdS/ZnS quantum dots confined in subwavelength polystyrene capsules. Uses non-polarized, homogeneously broadened emission satisfying Dicke superradiance description. Analytic relation connects second-order photon correlation to emitter number and collective lifetime.
AI.result: Developed analytic relation describing numerical dependence of second-order photon correlation on emitter number and collective lifetime. Achieved experimental counting range of colloidal quantum dots from one to ten.
AI.conclusion: Provides robust pathway for non-invasive numbering of artificial atoms and investigation of collective light-matter interactions at nanoscale using quantum optical techniques.

title: Ideal random quantum circuits pass the LXEB test
summary: We show that noiseless random quantum circuits pass the linear cross-entropy benchmark (LXEB) test with high probability. If the circuits are linear depth, and thus form unitary 4-designs, the LXEB test is passed with probability $1-O(1/\sqrt{k})$, where $k$ is the number of independently drawn samples from the output distribution of the random circuit. If the circuits are of depth $\tilde O(n^2)$, and thus form unitary $n$-designs, the LXEB test is passed with probability $1-O(e^{-k \log(n)/n})$. In proving our results, we show strong concentration of the random circuit collision probability at linear depth and establish that the tails of the distribution of random circuit output probabilities start to resemble Porter-Thomas at near-quadratic depths. Our analysis employs higher moments and high-degree approximate designs.

AI.tldr: Noiseless random quantum circuits pass the linear cross-entropy benchmark (LXEB) test with high probability, with success rates depending on circuit depth and sample size.
AI.motivation: To establish rigorous performance guarantees for random quantum circuits in passing the linear cross-entropy benchmark, which is important for demonstrating quantum computational advantage and characterizing the output distributions of random quantum circuits.
AI.method: Analyzes noiseless random quantum circuits at different depths: linear-depth circuits (forming unitary 4-designs) and near-quadratic-depth circuits (forming unitary n-designs). Uses higher moments and high-degree approximate designs to prove concentration properties of collision probability and output probability distributions.
AI.result: Linear-depth circuits pass LXEB with probability 1-O(1/√k) where k is sample size. Near-quadratic-depth circuits (depth ~O(n²)) pass with probability 1-O(e^{-k log(n)/n}). Shows strong concentration of collision probability at linear depth and Porter-Thomas-like tail behavior at near-quadratic depths.
AI.conclusion: Random quantum circuits reliably pass the linear cross-entropy benchmark test, with success probability improving with circuit depth and sample size, providing theoretical foundations for quantum advantage experiments.

title: Effective Repulsive Action of Gravitational Quantum Superpositions Under Postselection
summary: A classic feature of gravity is that it is an attractive force. If a source mass is prepared in a localized (classical- like) state, it will cause another probe mass to move towards it. Here we consider the situation in which a source mass is prepared in a quantum superposition of distinct spatial states while a probe mass interacts with it. Conditional on the detection of the source mass in a specific state, the probe mass will be found to move away from the source mass (repulsion). This signifies the quantum superposition of gravitational forces acting on the probe mass and thereby the fact that spacetime can exist in quantum superpositions. The technique used is the repulsive effect arising from an anomalous negative weak value. A potential experimental implementation with spin bearing nanocrystals is outlined.

AI.tldr: Quantum superposition of source mass creates repulsive gravitational effect on probe mass via anomalous negative weak values, demonstrating quantum spacetime superpositions.
AI.motivation: To explore whether gravity can exhibit quantum superposition effects and whether spacetime itself can exist in quantum superpositions, challenging the classical notion of gravity as purely attractive.
AI.method: Using a source mass prepared in quantum superposition of distinct spatial states interacting with a probe mass, with detection conditioned on specific source states. The technique leverages anomalous negative weak values to produce repulsive effects.
AI.result: Conditional on detecting the source mass in specific states, the probe mass moves away from the source (repulsion), demonstrating quantum superposition of gravitational forces and quantum spacetime superpositions.
AI.conclusion: Gravity can exhibit quantum superposition effects, spacetime can exist in quantum superpositions, and anomalous negative weak values enable observation of repulsive gravitational effects in quantum regimes.

title: A matching decoder for bivariate bicycle codes
summary: The discovery of new quantum error-correcting codes that encode several logical qubits into relatively few physical qubits motivates the development of efficient and accurate methods of decoding these systems. Here, we adopt the minimum-weight perfect matching algorithm, a subroutine invaluable to decoding topological codes, to decode bivariate bicycle codes. Using the equivalence of bivariate bicycle codes to copies of the toric code, we propose a method we call the 'cylinder trick' to rapidly find a correction using matching on code symmetries. We benchmark our decoder on the gross code family, cyclic hypergraph-product codes, generalized toric codes, and recently proposed directional codes, demonstrating the general applicability of our protocol. For a subset of these codes, we find that our decoder can be significantly improved by augmenting matching with strategies including belief propagation and 'over-matching', thus achieving performance competitive with state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) to decode bivariate bicycle codes via a 'cylinder trick' that exploits their equivalence to toric code copies, achieving competitive performance with belief propagation and 'over-matching' enhancements.
AI.motivation: New quantum error-correcting codes that encode multiple logical qubits into few physical qubits require efficient, accurate decoding methods. Existing MWPM algorithms work well for topological codes but need adaptation for bivariate bicycle codes.
AI.method: Adopt MWPM algorithm for bivariate bicycle codes by exploiting their equivalence to toric code copies. Introduce 'cylinder trick' to rapidly find corrections via matching on code symmetries. Augment with belief propagation and 'over-matching' strategies for improved performance.
AI.result: Benchmarked decoder on gross code family, cyclic hypergraph-product codes, generalized toric codes, and directional codes, demonstrating general applicability. For some codes, enhanced decoder with belief propagation and over-matching achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.conclusion: The cylinder trick enables efficient MWPM-based decoding of bivariate bicycle codes by leveraging their topological structure. Augmentation with belief propagation and over-matching yields competitive performance, providing a versatile decoding protocol for various quantum error-correcting codes.

title: Optimization-based Unfolding in High-Energy Physics
